## Quantitative Implications {#sec-valuation}

The quantitative implications come in three layers, ordered by how little they depend on the calibration: the allocation and its thresholds, Dario's dilemma, and credit risk at the model's policies. All magnitudes here are computed under the stylized calibration of @sec-calibration and illustrate the model's mechanisms rather than delivering point estimates. Internet Appendix G adds a unit-free scale-gap diagnostic motivated by @berk1999optimal (@fig-growth-decomposition).

### Allocation and Its Thresholds

Three objects are available in closed form and do not require (A2): the optimal training fraction $\phi^*$ of Proposition 1(i) and the thresholds $\underline{\phi}$ and $\tilde{\phi}$ of Proposition 2(ii), $0.70$, $0.18$ and $0.32$ at baseline. Perturbing each of the nine baseline parameters by $\pm 25\%$, one at a time, moves them within $\phi^* \in [0.59, 0.79]$, $\underline{\phi} \in [0.10, 0.23]$ and $\tilde{\phi} \in [0.19, 0.37]$, and the ordering $\underline{\phi} < \tilde{\phi} < \phi^*$ (faith-based survival at the optimal allocation) holds in each of the twelve draws that are solved. In a joint sweep of $4{,}096$ draws in the same box it holds in $99.2\%$ of the $1{,}910$ draws that are solved (Internet Appendix E, @tbl-joint-sweep). Triggers and capacities are objects of a different kind. They exist only under (A2), which excludes $53\%$ of the joint draws, and inside that window they are steep (@sec-calibration): $K^*$ covers almost thirteen orders of magnitude across the solved joint draws. I therefore report the levels of $X^*$, $K^*$, $X_L$ and $K_L$ as illustrations of the baseline, and rest the quantitative claims below on unit-free quantities.

### Dario's Dilemma

I now quantify Dario's dilemma, the cost of investing on a belief about the switch that differs from the truth.

Consider a firm that invests on a belief $\lambda_{\text{invest}}$ when the true arrival rate is $\lambda_{\text{true}}$. The model takes $\lambda_{\text{invest}}$ as given and prices the mismatch rather than deriving it from agency problems, signaling, or bounded rationality. The mistaken firm follows the policy that its belief prescribes in the exact problem of @sec-single-firm. With the post-switch scale precommitted (Proposition 1(iii)) every belief has a finite pre-switch trigger, so an error in either direction is an investment error; I take this version as the main one. With scale chosen at the switch, a firm that believes $\lambda \geq 0.073$ waits for the switch, as the correctly informed firm does at baseline. I report both, and then the same exercise inside the entry equilibrium of @sec-duopoly.

The value loss from mismatch is
$$
\Delta V = V(\lambda_{\text{true}}, \lambda_{\text{true}}) - V(\lambda_{\text{true}}, \lambda_{\text{invest}}),
$$
where $V(\lambda_a, \lambda_b)$ is the exact value under the arrival rate $\lambda_a$, at a reference demand $X_0$ at which the firm has not invested, of the policy that is optimal under $\lambda_b$. Losses are reported as $\Delta V / V(\lambda_{\text{true}}, \lambda_{\text{true}})$. The percentage is not invariant to $X_0$: I set $X_0 = X^*(\lambda_{\text{true}})/2$ and report $X^*/4$ and $3X^*/4$ in Internet Appendix A. Two errors can be called equal in three ways: equal differences in $\lambda$, equal ratios (equal differences in $\log \lambda$), or equal differences in the expected time to the switch $1/\lambda$. Internet Appendix A lists the pairs of beliefs used for each (@tbl-dilemma-pairs).

**Numerical Finding 1** (Dario's dilemma). *At the baseline calibration with $\lambda_{\text{true}} = 0.10$ and values measured at $X_0 = X^*/2$, the single firm with precommitted post-switch scale loses $32\%$ of its value by investing as if $\lambda = 0.02$ and $1.3\%$ by investing as if $\lambda = 0.18$: for equal errors in the level of $\lambda$ the pessimistic error costs about twenty-five times the optimistic one. For equal proportional errors the pessimistic error still costs more, by a much smaller factor: $32\%$ against $13\%$ at a factor of five ($\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.02$ and $0.50$), and $4.3\%$ against $1.3\%$ at a factor of $1.8$. For equal errors in the expected time to the switch the two are about equal, the optimist losing slightly more: $1.0\%$ for the pessimist against $1.3\%$ for the optimist at $4.4$ years. With scale chosen at the switch the comparison is one-sided: every belief at or above $0.073$ prescribes waiting for the switch, which is what the correctly informed firm does, and costs nothing, while $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.02$ costs $41\%$. These are numerical results on a grid: the baseline parameters, eleven beliefs between $0.02$ and $0.50$, and reference demands $X^*/4$, $X^*/2$ and $3X^*/4$ (@tbl-dilemma, @tbl-dilemma-pairs). At true rates of $0.05$ and $0.20$ the rankings in levels and at a factor of five hold; at a factor of $1.8$ and in expected time the pessimist loses more at $0.05$ and the optimist at $0.20$ (Internet Appendix A).*

The largest component of the loss is the training allocation, on both sides. Of the pessimist's $32$ points at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.02$, allocation accounts for $24$ and timing for $8$; of the far optimist's $13$ points at $0.50$, allocation accounts for $8$, capacity for $4$ and timing for $1.5$ (Internet Appendix A). Allocation dominates on the pessimistic side because of an identity: at $\phi^*$ the post-switch term is a share $\phi^*$ of $A_{\text{eff}}$, $70\%$ at baseline, so a firm that trains with $14\%$ of its capacity gives up most of what an installed firm is worth, whereas a firm that trains with $97\%$ gives up inference revenue and keeps the post-switch claim. The pessimist does not invest late: its own trigger lies far below $X_0$, and it invests at once at a third of the informed firm's capacity, so it errs in the allocation and by investing too early for the truth, not too late. Capacity also responds to beliefs: the optimist at $0.18$ installs $17\%$ more than the informed firm, and the optimist at $0.50$ installs the same capacity at a trigger $29\%$ lower. The pure-power approximation understates the pessimist's loss and overstates the optimists' ($26\%$, $4.1\%$ and $23\%$ at the three beliefs; @tbl-dilemma).

@fig-investment-dilemma plots the loss against $\lambda_{\text{invest}}$ on a logarithmic axis, on which equal proportional errors are equidistant from the truth. In panel (a) the loss under precommitted scale rises on both sides of $\lambda_{\text{true}}$ and more steeply on the pessimistic side; with scale chosen at the switch it is zero to the right of $0.073$. Fairly priced leverage leaves the losses almost unchanged: with the policies held at the unlevered ones, they move by at most $0.1$ point between zero leverage and $0.40$. Under par debt the financing subsidy rewards scale, and the pessimist's loss rises to $35\%$ at $\ell = 0.40$ (@tbl-dilemma-tail).

Expected value is not the only margin. Each mistaken firm enters closer than the informed firm to the boundary at which it stops operating. The informed single firm enters at $6.5$ times that boundary; the optimist with $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.50$ enters at $4.1$ times, because its trigger is lower and its allocation depresses the pre-switch revenue that covers operating costs. The five-year probability of reaching the boundary (a first passage under the L-regime drift that omits the switch, and therefore an upper bound on the pre-switch probability) is $0.16\%$ for the informed firm without debt, $0.37\%$ and $0.34\%$ at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.02$ and $0.18$, and $1.8\%$ at $0.50$. At $\ell = 0.40$ under fairly priced debt these become $0.47\%$, $0.71\%$, $1.0\%$ and $4.3\%$ (@tbl-dilemma-tail). For the far optimist the belief matters more than leverage: its probability is about eleven times the informed firm's without any debt and nine times at $\ell = 0.40$. Errors of $0.08$ in either direction leave the two firms about equally likely to reach the boundary, and an error of a factor of five leaves the optimist with five times the pessimist's probability.

Panel (a): the single firm, valued exactly at $X_0 = X^*/2$ on a finer grid of $121$ beliefs between $0.015$ and $0.50$, with the post-switch scale precommitted (solid) and with scale chosen at the switch (dashed); the dotted curve is the pure-power approximation. Moderate optimism is cheap in this calibration, and a belief five times the truth is not: it costs $13\%$ in expected value and multiplies the probability of reaching the shutdown boundary by eleven. A moderately optimistic belief could thus account for large investment at a small cost in expected value. The exercise compares point mismatches and averages over no prior, so it illustrates rather than identifies beliefs.

The single firm is the monopoly case. Inside the entry equilibrium of @sec-duopoly, one firm holds the belief $\lambda_{\text{invest}}$ and its rival holds the truth and best-responds (Internet Appendix E, @tbl-duopoly-dilemma). A mistaken leader loses more than the single firm on both sides, and the far optimist's loss grows most: $48\%$ at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.02$, $1.8\%$ at $0.18$ and $32\%$ at $0.50$, measured at $X_0 = X_L/2$, so the pessimistic error costs twenty-seven times the optimistic one in levels and $1.5$ times at a factor of five. A mistaken follower that remains a follower loses nothing, because the follower's post-switch policy does not involve $\lambda$; on the grid that is the case for beliefs between $0.075$ and $0.30$, and outside that range the mistaken firm takes the lead and bears a loss close to the leader's. The leader's tail exposure is larger than the single firm's: without debt the five-year probability is $0.84\%$ for the informed leader and $8.7\%$ at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.50$.

### Credit Risk at the Model's Policies

Credit risk is evaluated where the model's firms invest. Debt is issued at three entries: the single firm's precommitted-scale entry $(X^*, K^*, \phi^*)$ of Proposition 1(iii); the duopoly's first investment $(X_L, K_L, \phi_L)$, with the leader's policy held at its unlevered equilibrium value; and the follower's post-switch entry. It is priced with the exact claims of @sec-duopoly under par and fairly priced debt (Internet Appendix H, @tbl-credit-spread, @tbl-credit-pd, @fig-credit-risk). Three numerical results follow. First, at these policies credit risk is the risk of reaching a boundary that operating costs create without any debt, and leverage shifts that boundary. The operating-cost claim $\delta K/r$ is twelve times the par coupon claim at $\ell = 0.40$ for the single firm and twenty-three times for the leader, so the spread on an infinitesimal issue is already $22$ basis points for the single firm and $44$ for the leader, and leverage of $0.40$ adds about $4$ basis points to each under par debt and about $11$ under fairly priced debt. The five-year probabilities of reaching the boundary are $0.16\%$ and $0.84\%$ without debt, and $0.47\%$ and $1.45\%$ at $\ell = 0.40$ under fairly priced debt. Second, the firm most exposed is the leader, which enters at $4.8$ times its shutdown boundary against $6.5$ for the single firm and ten for the follower, on whose infinitesimal issue the spread is $4$ basis points. Third, recovery plays almost no part. It is at most $5\%$ of the coupon claim at these policies for $\ell \leq 0.70$, so the loss given default is $95\%$ or more, and at a fixed scale more training raises recovery rather than lowering it (@fig-credit-risk, panel c). Over $\phi \in [0.30, 0.75]$ the spread falls as $\phi$ rises, for the single firm and the leader under both debt conventions. Spreads and default probabilities are model-implied risk-adjusted objects rather than risk-neutral quantities, and the leverage gradients describe the response to an imposed debt burden at a fixed policy (@sec-conventions).
